Correlations. The homogeneity test for the 27 correlations from 
the EEO data was significant, QT(26) = 252.78, p < .001, indicat-
ing that the effects do not represent a single population.10 The 
weighted average effect under the random-effects model for these 
27 data points was .18 (SE = .028), with a 95% confidence inter-
val (CI) from .12 to .23. All of the studies that used EEO data 
reported correlations by race and school level; some computed 
mean effects by race (White, Black) and school level (elementary/
middle, high school). Table 2 shows that three of the groups were 
heterogeneous and that one, White high school students, was 
homogeneous (and thus was analyzed via a fixed-effects model). 
The pattern of the means suggested an interaction effect between 
race and school level, as shown in the plot of the four means in 
Figure 1. Thus we included four effects to represent the EEO data 
in the full analysis, for the four race × school-level groups.11 The 
reduced data set was slightly less variable than the original set of 
values, but the mean of the set of four effects (.17) was nearly equal 
to the original mean of .18. We analyzed these four average effects 
representing the EEO data set together with the 13 correlations 
not based on EEO data, creating a full data set of 17 correlations.

As mentioned, other alternative models were tested. In model 2, a direct line was added between secure attachment and leadership
experiences. As presented in Fig. 3, the model ﬁtted the data well: a non-signiﬁcant χ2 was obtained (54.77; df=49; p=.27), all ﬁt
indexes exceeded .90, and the RMSEA was signiﬁcant (p<.05). However, the additional direct relation between secure attachment and
leadership experiences was not signiﬁcant (β=.18, p=.12). Moreover, the relation between trait anxiety and leadership experiences
was not signiﬁcant (β=−.11, p<.05).
To test the differences between the two models a chi-square difference test was conducted and was found not signiﬁcant
(χ2=2.36, df=1, p=.12). These ﬁndings suggest that this alternative model made no signiﬁcant contribution and was less adequate
in explaining the relations between the variables.
Another alternative model suggested that three independent variables (secure attachment, trait anxiety and openness to
experiences) were directly related to the dependent variable (model 3). As presented in Fig. 4, the model did not ﬁt the data well:
a signiﬁcant χ2 was obtained (132.1; df=51; p=.00), most ﬁt indexes did not exceed .90, and the RMSEA was not signiﬁcant
